bodyHtml:
What is ASME Section V (ASME Section 5)?

ASME Section V, also written ASME Section 5, ASME V or BPVC.V, is the nondestructive examination volume of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code. It sets out how to perform RT, UT, PT, MT, ET, VT, leak testing and other methods: equipment, calibration, technique, written procedures, personnel and records. It applies only when another code section or a contract invokes it. It never sets acceptance criteria. The current edition is 2025.

ASME Section V article by article

Section V is organized in subsections. Subsection A holds the method articles ASME writes. Subsection B republishes ASTM standards as SE- and SA- documents, which are generally for reference unless a method article or the referencing code calls them. The 2025 edition added a Subsection C for in-service techniques and moved several existing articles into it. Article numbers below follow recent editions. Check the edition your contract names before you cite a number in a procedure.

ArticleMethodWhat it requires, in general terms
1General requirementsWho is responsible for what, the Manufacturer or user versus the Inspector. Personnel qualified to an employer's written practice. Written procedures, and demonstration of them, when the referencing code requires. Equipment calibration and records. Mandatory Appendix II adds supplemental personnel qualification for techniques such as PAUT, TOFD, computed and digital radiography.
2Radiographic examinationSource, film or detector selection. Image quality indicator (IQI) selection and placement. Density or digital image quality. Location markers and technique sketches. Appendices cover digital image acquisition and storage, phosphor imaging plates and castings.
4Ultrasonic examination of weldsA procedure whose essential variables are listed in table form. Calibration blocks by thickness and curvature. Instrument linearity checks (Mandatory Appendices I and II). Sensitivity setting, scanning coverage and recording levels. Mandatory appendices for TOFD (III), phased array with manual raster scanning (IV), encoded E-scan and S-scan phased array (V) and UT procedure qualification (IX).
5Ultrasonic examination of materialsPlate, forgings, castings, bolting, pumps and valves, and thickness measurement. Straight-beam and angle-beam calibration for each product form.
6Liquid penetrant examinationProcedure variables, contaminant limits for penetrant materials used on nickel alloys, austenitic stainless and titanium, dwell and development times, lighting, and qualification for temperatures outside the standard range.
7Magnetic particle examinationYoke, prod, coil and central-conductor techniques. Field adequacy checks with field indicators or artificial-flaw shims. Particle concentration and lighting. An appendix for AC yokes on ferritic material under nonmagnetic coatings.
8Eddy current examinationAppendices for nonferromagnetic heat-exchanger tubing, coated ferritic materials, external-coil examination of tubular products, coating thickness, and surface-crack depth with surface probes.
9Visual examinationDirect and remote visual technique, lighting, access, a procedure demonstration showing the technique resolves fine detail, and personnel vision requirements.
10Leak testingBubble, halogen, helium mass spectrometer, pressure change and ultrasonic leak detector techniques, each with a sensitivity check.
11 and 12Acoustic emissionArticle 11 covers fiber-reinforced plastic vessels. Article 12 covers metallic vessels during pressure testing. Both set instrumentation, sensor placement, stressing sequence and evaluation.
13Continuous acoustic emission monitoringLong-term monitoring of pressure boundaries, with system calibration. Relocated to Subsection C in 2025.
14Examination system qualificationStatistically based performance demonstration, covering probability of detection and false calls, for when a referencing code requires a qualified system.
15, 16 and 17ACFM, magnetic flux leakage and remote field testingTechnique-specific procedure tables, reference plates or tubes, and calibration. ACFM (Article 15) was relocated to Subsection C in 2025.
18 and 19Acoustic pulse reflectometry; guided wave examination of pipingTube-bundle and piping screening techniques. Both were relocated to Subsection C in 2025.
20 and 21Computed tomography; pulsed eddy current for corrosion screeningBoth were added in the 2021 edition. PEC includes a technical feasibility evaluation before use, and moved to Subsection C in 2025.
Subsection BAdopted ASTM standardsSE- and SA- versions of ASTM guides, practices and specifications for each method. They become mandatory only when invoked.

If you have seen a list that starts with "Article 1: Visual" or places phased array in Article 11, it is wrong. Article 1 is general requirements. Phased array and TOFD sit inside Article 4 as mandatory appendices. Article 3 was emptied long ago when its radiography content merged into Article 2. The 2025 reorganization also moved full matrix capture out of Article 4, so FMC procedures need their code address checked.

How construction codes invoke Section V

Section V does nothing on its own. A construction code or a contract has to call it, and the call works as a chain:

  1. The construction code decides that an examination is required. Section I for power boilers, Section VIII Divisions 1 and 2 for pressure vessels, Section III for nuclear components, B31.1 for power piping, B31.3 for process piping.
  2. The construction code sets the extent and the acceptance criteria. How many welds, what percentage, which method, and what is rejectable. For example, B31.3 sets examination extent by fluid service, and Section VIII Division 1 sets when full radiography is required (UW-11) and how it is judged (UW-51).
  3. The construction code points to the Section V article for technique. B31.3 sends radiography to Article 2, ultrasonic examination to Article 4, penetrant to Article 6, magnetic particle to Article 7 and visual to Article 9. Section VIII does the same through its radiography paragraphs and its MT and PT appendices.
  4. Article 1 then tells you what the referencing code must supply. That covers personnel qualification, extent of examination, acceptance standards, record retention and reporting. If the referencing code is silent on one of these, the contract has to fill the gap.

In-service work follows a parallel path. API 510, API 570, API 653 and the National Board Inspection Code (NBIC) govern inspection and repair of equipment already in service, and they refer back to Section V for examination technique in their repair and alteration rules. On those jobs the owner's Authorized Inspector stays inspector of record. Atlantis delivers the NDE to that inspector and is not the Authorized Inspector. One frequent surprise: structural steel welded to AWS D1.1 does not run through Section V at all. D1.1 carries its own UT and PAUT requirements.

For code-by-code detail, see B31.3 examination extent by fluid service and Section VIII Division 1 RT and UT acceptance criteria.

Written procedures and demonstration

When the referencing code requires it, every Section V examination runs to a written procedure. The procedure must be demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Inspector, which in practice means the Authorized Inspector working for the Manufacturer's inspection agency. Four points decide whether a procedure survives review.

Essential and nonessential variables

Most method articles carry a table of procedure requirements, each marked essential or nonessential. You can find them in Article 4 for UT of welds, Article 6 for PT, Article 7 for MT and Article 9 for VT. Change an essential variable, such as the penetrant family, the UT instrument or a search unit outside the qualified range, and the procedure must be requalified by demonstration. Change a nonessential variable and you revise the document, but you do not need to demonstrate again.

What a demonstration record should show

  • Procedure number and revision, and the Section V edition it was written to
  • Equipment by serial number, search units or consumables by batch, and calibration blocks by identification
  • The demonstration specimen and the indications it contains
  • Personnel who performed it, with certification level
  • Results, and the Inspector's acceptance with date and signature

Formal procedure qualification

Some techniques need more than a demonstration. When UT is used for flaw sizing, or the acceptance criteria are fracture-mechanics based, Article 4's procedure qualification appendix calls for qualification on blocks with known flaws. Article 14 applies when the referencing code demands a statistically qualified examination system. Budget for qualification blocks early. Blocks with real or simulated flaws have long lead times.

Approval

A certified Level III approves the procedure, and the approval should state the certification basis. Our Section V procedure writing guide covers structure. Article-level detail for UT is in the Article 4 requirements explainer.

Personnel qualification references: SNT-TC-1A, CP-189 and central certification

Article 1 requires NDE personnel to be qualified and certified to their employer's written practice. That practice must follow one of two ASNT documents:

  • SNT-TC-1A, a recommended practice. The employer adapts its training hours, experience and exam content in the written practice and can justify changes.
  • ANSI/ASNT CP-189, a consensus standard. It is more prescriptive. For example, the Level III must hold ASNT Level III certification, and training outlines come from ANSI/ASNT CP-105.

The comparison is laid out in SNT-TC-1A vs CP-189. Three details catch employers out:

  • Each Section V edition fixes which edition of the ASNT document applies. The 2025 Code adopts the 2024 edition of SNT-TC-1A. A Section V interpretation reported by HSB confirms that written practices do not have to meet the May 2025 addendum to it. Certifications earned under a prior edition generally remain valid until recertification. New and renewed certifications follow the adopted edition.
  • Central certification can satisfy part of the requirement. Section V lets a national or international central certification scheme satisfy some written-practice requirements. ASNT's ACCP has been replaced by the ASNT 9712 program, launched in March 2023, and the ACCP transition period runs to September 2028. ISO 9712 certification can also be used. The employer still issues the certification under its written practice.
  • Advanced techniques need supplemental qualification. Article 1 Mandatory Appendix II adds technique-specific training, experience and examinations for PAUT, TOFD, computed radiography and digital radiography. A UT Level II without these records should not interpret PAUT data on Code work that invokes Article 1.

Canada note: provinces adopt ASME construction codes through CSA B51 and their own regulations, enforced by authorities such as TSSA in Ontario and ABSA in Alberta. Section V therefore applies to Canadian Code work much as it does in the US. Many Canadian owners also require personnel certified to CAN/CGSB-48.9712. CGSB closed on April 1, 2026, and NRCan's NDT Certification Body continues to issue that certification.

The Section V edition cycle

  • Every two years, in odd years. ASME stopped publishing addenda and moved to a new edition every two years. The 2025 edition was published on July 1, 2025. The next is due in 2027.
  • Six months to comply. A new edition becomes mandatory six months after issue. The 2025 edition became mandatory on January 1, 2026.
  • Errata and notices between editions. HSB counted at least 30 errata and notices against the July 2025 Code within months of issue. Some changed requirements, not just typography. Subscribe to ASME's errata notices or have your Level III track them.
  • Code cases and interpretations. Code cases permit alternatives before they are written into the Code. Interpretations answer specific questions. Neither changes your procedure unless you invoke it, but auditors expect you to know the relevant ones.

For new construction, the Section V edition follows the construction code edition on the contract and data report. For in-service work, the owner's procedures name the edition. When an edition changes, run a gap analysis on every procedure and the written practice inside the six-month window, then record the effective date of each revision.

Common Section V audit findings beyond expired certifications

Expired certifications and generic procedures are the findings everyone knows. These are the ones we see next, in procedure reviews and client audits:

  1. Stale article addresses. Procedures that cite FMC, PEC, ACFM, APR or guided wave by an article number the 2025 edition has moved.
  2. Written practice behind the Code. The written practice still names SNT-TC-1A 2020 after the contract moved to the 2025 Code.
  3. No Appendix II records. PAUT, TOFD, CR or DR technicians with method certification but no supplemental technique qualification on file.
  4. Essential variable changed without requalification. A new penetrant family, a different UT instrument or a probe frequency outside the demonstrated range, with no new demonstration.
  5. Demonstration without the Inspector. The procedure was demonstrated, but nothing shows the Inspector witnessed or accepted it.
  6. Calibration blocks that do not match. Wrong material group, thickness or curvature for the component examined.
  7. Linearity checks missing. Article 4 Mandatory Appendices I and II not documented at the interval the article requires.
  8. No contaminant certifications. PT materials used on austenitic stainless or nickel alloy with no batch certification for sulfur and halogen content.
  9. Unverified MT fields. Field strength never verified with an indicator or shims, or yoke lifting-power checks overdue.
  10. Subsection B misread. An ASTM SE- document treated as mandatory when nothing invokes it, or ignored when the article does invoke it.

Frequently asked questions

Is ASME Section 5 the same as ASME Section V and ASME V?

Yes. Section V, Section 5, ASME V, Sec V and BPVC.V all refer to the same volume, Nondestructive Examination, of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code. ASME numbers its sections with Roman numerals, so "Section 5" is the informal spelling.

What is the current edition of ASME Section V?

The 2025 edition, published July 1, 2025, and mandatory from January 1, 2026. It added Subsection C for in-service techniques and adopted the 2024 edition of SNT-TC-1A. The next edition is due in 2027.

How many articles are in ASME Section V?

Subsection A has run from Article 1 to Article 21 in recent editions, with no Article 3 for many years. Subsection B starts at Article 22 and holds the adopted ASTM standards. The 2025 edition moved several in-service articles into a new Subsection C, so count against the edition you hold.

Does ASME Section V apply to in-service inspection under API 510, 570 or 653?

Indirectly. The API inspection codes and the NBIC refer to Section V for examination technique, especially for repairs and alterations. Owners' in-service procedures often cite it too. Acceptance and inspection intervals still come from the API code and the owner's program, under the owner's Authorized Inspector.

Does ASME Section V accept ISO 9712 or ASNT 9712 certification?

Partly. Section V allows a central certification scheme to satisfy some of the written practice requirements, and it names the employer's written practice as the basis of certification. ASNT 9712 or ISO 9712 certificates support that practice. They do not replace it.

Is ASME Section V required for AWS D1.1 structural welds?

No. AWS D1.1 has its own examination and personnel requirements, including a phased array annex added in its 2020 edition. Section V applies when an ASME code, or a contract, invokes it.

Who is responsible for Section V compliance on a job?

The Code user, typically the Manufacturer or the owner, holds overall responsibility, including personnel qualification under its quality program. An NDE subcontractor is responsible for its own procedures, personnel and records, and those must meet the user's requirements. The Authorized Inspector verifies. Put the split in writing in the subcontract.

What changed in the 2025 edition of ASME Section V?

The main changes for US users are a new Subsection C that groups in-service techniques, relocation of several articles into it, full matrix capture moving out of Article 4, adoption of SNT-TC-1A 2024, and a series of errata after issue. Check any procedure that cites an article number or an ASNT edition.
